DAY 02 OF 09 · SAT 28 NOV
EQUATOR DAY

Quito

2,850 m
Two cars, two starts: the crater hikers leave first, Ben's car follows, and everyone meets on the crater rim before the fog. Then the real equator, a sunset over the old town and the first special dinner. Mike lands in the afternoon and joins at dinner.
TWO CARS, TWO STARTSThe crater car takes breakfast to go; Ben's car has breakfast at the penthouse.07:30 · The crater car leaves the penthouse first: down into Pululahua crater and back up to the rim before the ~11:30 fog. Start back up by 09:30 at the latest.~09:00–09:15 · Ben's car leaves the penthouse and drives straight to the Ventanillas viewpoint. No airport run.~10:15–10:30 · Meet at Mirador de Ventanillas, Pululahua; lunch at El Cráter at 12:00.
THE DAY
07:30
The crater car leaves first, breakfast to go, to walk down into Pululahua crater (1.7 km each way, ~350 m climb back) and back up on the rim before the ~11:30 fog. Start back up by 09:30 at the latest.
09:00
Ben's car leaves the penthouse (~09:00–09:15) and drives straight to the Ventanillas viewpoint, about 1 h–1 h 15. No airport run.
~10:15
Pululahua, Mirador de Ventanillas. Both cars meet here ~10:15–10:30. Viewpoint until the 11:30 fog cut; the hikers are back up by then. Lunch at El Cráter next.
12:00
Lunch at El Cráter on the rim (reserve a crater-view table)
13:15
Intiñán & Mitad del Mundo, to ~15:15. Then MegaMaxi ~16:00 for Tena staples.
17:45
El Panecillo by taxi for the 18:05 sunset. Skip if pouring.
18:45
La Ronda, then special dinner #1 at Casa Gangotena, 19:45. Mike joins here: he lands at UIO 16:05 and takes an official taxi or Uber (~$20–30, 45–90 min) to the penthouse, there ~17:30–18:00.
THE CARS
Two midsize SUVs (Nissan Kicks or similar, manual), collected Fri 27. Plates not ending 7 or 8. Card hold (~$2,000–3,000) in the main driver's name. Fill both tonight (Caspigasi, Calacalí road).
PARKING
Penthouse has one space: car #2 to a staffed paid lot. Taxis into the Centre tonight (Fiestas closures).
TAXI, NOT STAIRS
El Panecillo: taxi up and have it wait (~$10–15). Never the stairway.
SLEEPING
Penthouse, night 2. Pack tonight: departure 07:00, checkout 11:00.
TOMORROW · SUN 29 NOV · TO TENA
07:00 over the Papallacta Pass (4,060 m, near freezing). Guango feeders 08:45–10:15, Baeza coffee, lunch at El Bambú, Tena ~13:00.
DAY 02 · SAT 28 NOV · 07:30–11:30
PLACE CARD

Pululahua

Crater
rim lookout ~2,900 m
A collapsed volcano with a farming community still living on the crater floor. The name means “cloud of water”.
SPLIT CARS: HIKE OR VIEWPOINT
One car does the crater-floor walk (1.7 km each way, ~350 m climb back up; leave at 07:30, start back up by 09:30 at the latest); the other stays at the viewpoint, hard cut 11:30 before the fog. Everyone regroups for lunch on the rim.
AT THE RIM
1
Mirador de Ventanillas: the lookout over the patchwork farms, ~40 families still living on the floor.
FREE ⚠ · REGISTER AT THE RANGER POST
2
Look out for sparkling violetear on the shrubs, American kestrel over the fields.
3
Lunch at El Cráter on the rim ~12:00: reserve a crater-view table (+593 99 733 9406; ask about locro).
BACKUP: BALCÓN AL MUNDO
GETTING THERE
From the penthouse: north past Mitad del Mundo, ~1 h–1 h 15. Small roadside parking.
WEAR
Fleece (chilly in the fog), sunscreen, hat. Nothing visible in the cars.
WATER
~2,900 m: water in hand, no exertion.
NEXT → Intiñán and Mitad del Mundo from 13:15, 10 min back down the road. Both are fog-proof.

DAY 03 · SUN 29 NOV · 08:45–10:15
PLACE CARD

Guango

Lodge
cloud forest ~2,700 m
A hummingbird lodge about 10 km past Papallacta, right on the road to Tena. Ninety minutes at the feeders and the river, with coffee.
PLANNED STOP, 90 MIN
Feeders, riverside trails, coffee and a snack. Walk-in ~$5 with coffee, cash. Email info@guangolodge.com the week before (7–8 people, ~08:45).
WHAT YOU'LL SEE
1
Sword-billed hummingbird (60–70%), the only bird whose bill is longer than its body. Collared inca, coronets and sylphs near-certain.
AT THE FEEDERS
2
Torrent duck and white-capped dipper on the river rocks behind the lodge.
3
Before it, at 08:15: the La Virgen pass, ~4,060 m. Curiquingue by the road, a condor if you're lucky.
PULL OUT ONLY IF CLEAR · STAY BY THE CARS
COST
~$5 each with coffee (~$35 for 7). Cash.
WEATHER
~8–15 °C, drizzle and mist: rain jacket, fleece, binoculars.
REGROUP
Both cars meet here, then at Baeza's “La Y”.
NEXT → Baeza 10:45 for toilets, coffee and fuel; lunch at El Bambú, Cotundo, 12:45.

DAY 04 · MON 30 NOV · 09:30–10:30
PLACE CARD

amaZOOnico

Rescue centre
Río Napo · ~400 m
A rescue centre on the Napo for animals taken from the pet trade, reached by motor canoe. One guided hour, animals in care only.
TIMED · CANOE DETAILS PENDING
Visitors 08:30–14:00 daily; our slot is 09:30. Reservation via their Google Form, canoe via Liana Lodge (+593 6 301 7702). Leave the house 08:00, park at Puerto Barantilla ~09:00. The canoe booking, price and pick-up details are still pending.
WHAT TO EXPECT
1
The guided hour: capuchin and woolly monkeys, tapir, ocelot, macaws and river turtles, all in care, with the guide, then time for questions and the shop.
2
From the canoe: great egret and cocoi heron on the sandbars, kingfishers on low branches, black caracara on dead trees.
3
The rules: no touching, talking to or feeding; no flash; stay on the path and with the group.
ENTRY
$5 each, cash. Canoe fare unpublished; cash too.
GETTING THERE
~1 h from the house via Puerto Napo, then ~10 min by canoe. Windows shut at the landing.
BRING
Dry bag, hat, strapped sandals, SPF 50, poncho. Boots lent.
Open to everyone unless the booking reply says free-roaming primates approach the path; then the unvaccinated do the enclosures only.
NEXT → Canoe back ~10:45–11:00, then Misahuallí: a short Monkey Beach stop and lunch in town, ~12:00–13:30. Sinchi Warmi from 14:00.
DAY 04 · MON 30 NOV · 14:00–16:00
PLACE CARD

Sinchi
Warmi

Kichwa women's lodge
near Misahuallí
A non-profit lodge run by Kichwa women since 2002. Our afternoon: ancestral medicine and a handicrafts workshop.
OFFER IN · NOT BOOKED YET
Asociación de Mujeres Kichwas Sinchi Warmi: our plan is now Mon 30 Nov, 14:00–~16:00. Pending: Sinchi Warmi to confirm the later start and the souvenir arrangement, then the 50% deposit. The date isn't held until the deposit is paid. WhatsApp +593 99 875 4861 or sinchiwarmis@gmail.com.
OUR AFTERNOON · 14:00–~16:00English-speaking guide, for our group.$20 · Ancestral medicine, knowledge sharing, 45 min$25 · Amazonian handicrafts, making a group souvenir, 1 hTotal $45 per person. No lunch included: lunch is in Misahuallí first. This replaces the earlier 12:30–15:30 maito-lunch offer.
THE AFTERNOON
1
Guayusa: the welcome tea. Chicha: a small sip, hand the bowl back (“Gracias, ya no”).
2
Ancestral medicine, 45 min: the women share their plant knowledge, under thatch and trees: blue morphos in sunny breaks, leafcutter ants, maybe a poison-dart frog (don't touch).
3
Handicrafts, 1 h: make a group souvenir. Buy, don't bargain. Say no to any limpia or ayahuasca add-on.
COST
$20 + $25 = $45 each, no lunch. Transfer + cash.
MONKEY BEACH
Wild capuchins grab bags and can bite. Open to everyone, your own call; keep your distance, never touch or feed. Rabies vaccine recommended.
WORDS
Alli puncha (good morning), pagarachu (thank you).
NEXT → Back at the house ~16:45–17:00 for the pool, jacuzzi from 18:00, dinner at Vagabundo or a BBQ at 19:00.

Omaere, Puyo (before): a guided medicinal-plant walk, 1–1.5 h. A learning walk, not a show.
$3 CASH · TUE–SUN 09:00–17:00

Pailón del Diablo: white-collared swifts swirl behind the falls; dippers on the wet rocks.
~$2–3 CASH · PAID GUARDED LOTS IN RÍO VERDE
3
Manto de la Novia (15 min, free; tarabita $2) and the Agoyán falls as a drive-by.

DAY 07 · THU 3 DEC · 10:20–11:30
PLACE CARD

Saquisilí

Thursday market
~2,900 m
A real locals' market across seven or eight plazas: produce, grains, textiles, hats. Thursday only, which is why we drive today.
HARD TIMES
70 minutes on site. If arrival slips past ~11:00, skip the market and go straight to Latacunga. Latest safe departure from Saquisilí: 13:15.
THE PLAZAS
1
Food stalls: hornado and empanadas de morocho, share a plate.
CASH ~$3–5
2
Textiles and hats: bargain gently for crafts, never for food.
3
Optional skips: the small-animal plaza (live cuy, puppies). The livestock market is over by 10:00.
PARKING
Paid lot on the edge; the streets jam. All luggage aboard, nothing visible.
MANNERS
“Buenos días”. Ask before photos (“¿Puedo tomarle una foto?”), accept a no. Don't film the animal sellers.
BRING
Hat, SPF 50, a fleece (~12 °C), small cash in a front pocket.
Yupaychani is thank you here (highland Kichwa).
NEXT → Lunch at La Mamá Negra, Latacunga: chugchucaras, big shared plates. Then the E35 north.

DECREE 498 · WHAT IT MEANS FOR US
SAFETY

Checkpoints

An estado de excepción lets the President suspend specific rights in named provinces and puts soldiers alongside the police. Since Jan 2024 Ecuador is also in an “internal armed conflict” with organised crime, so checkpoints are normal everywhere.
Decree 498
Signed 15 Sep 2026 by President Noboa; in force 15 Sep – 14 Nov (60 days, renewable once for 30). Reason: organised-crime expansion, 442 homicides in 8 provinces in 4 weeks.
Where
El Oro, Esmeraldas, Guayas, Los Ríos, Manabí, Pichincha, Santa Elena, Santo Domingo + 3 cantons.
On our route
Pichincha: Quito, Pululahua, the airport, Mindo, Tulipe. Not Napo (Tena), Tungurahua (Baños) or Cotopaxi (Saquisilí, Latacunga).
Rights limited
Home searches without a court order where there are signs of armed groups, weapons or drugs; individualised access to correspondence. Movement only under the coastal curfew.
Curfew
Guayas, Manabí, Los Ríos, El Oro only, 17–30 Sep, 00:00–05:00. No curfew in Pichincha. May 2026 had one in Quito (23:00–05:00) with airport trips exempt on proof of travel.
27 Nov – 5 Dec
Unknown. A 30-day renewal would run to ~14 Dec. Plan on Pichincha under a state of exception, without a curfew. Re-check after 14 Nov.
WHERE TO EXPECT THEM
Quito ring roads (28 Nov, 3 and 5 Dec) · Calacalí–Mindo road (3 and 5 Dec, plus the 04:00 run) · Pifo → La Virgen (29 Nov) · Machachi/Tambillo (3 Dec). Routine police at Baeza, the Tena, Puyo and Baños entries and Latacunga–Saquisilí.
AT A CHECKPOINT
Stop, windows down, hands visible, don’t film. Show licence + IDP + passport + matrícula + SOAT. Never offer money.
PASSPORTS
Everyone carries one; originals in the car on transfer days. Carry e-tickets on 5 Dec.
IF A CURFEW CAME
Dinners end ~21:30; airport runs rely on the exemption. Breaking it: up to 3 years.
PARO
A national strike can block roads (Oct 2025). Turn around rather than wait at a blockade.
THE RULE FOR WILD PRIMATES
HEALTH

Monkeys
& rabies

Monkey Beach is open to everyone, and going is each person's own call. Keep your distance; nobody touches or feeds any wildlife. Bites and scratches are each person's own responsibility. A pre-exposure rabies vaccine is recommended.
Misahuallí Monkey Beach, Mon 30
Open to everyone, your own call. Wild, food-habituated white-fronted capuchins grab bags and can bite. ~15 min stop: keep your distance, no food out, bags zipped. A pre-exposure rabies vaccine is recommended. Windows shut and nothing loose at the plaza and the canoe landing.
amaZOOnico, Mon 30
Rescued animals with a guide: open to everyone, keep distance, no touching, talking to or feeding, no flash. If the booking reply says free-roaming primates approach the path, the same rule as Monkey Beach applies: your own call, keep your distance.
Puyo and Baños
Skip Puyo’s monkey “paseo” and any street photo holding a sloth, boa or parrot. Mindo feeder gardens are fine; nobody hand-feeds birds.
BITE, SCRATCH OR LICK ON BROKEN SKIN · MONKEY, DOG, BAT
Wash 15 minutes with soap under running water. Povidone-iodine or alcohol. Don’t close the wound; ask about tetanus. Hospital the same day. Bring your vaccination record. MSP line 171 or 911.
PRE-VACCINATED
2 boosters, days 0 and 3. No immunoglobulin needed.
UNVACCINATED
RIG + 4 doses (days 0, 3, 7, 14). RIG may only be in Quito, 4–5 h from Tena: start the vaccine anyway, RIG can be added up to day 7.
WHERE TO GO
Tena
Hospital General José María Velasco Ibarra (MSP, 24 h)
Baños
Hospital Básico Baños (24 h); Ambato ~40 km for anything serious
Mindo
Centro de Salud (first aid only); PEP in Quito, ~2 h
Quito
Hospital Metropolitano; Hospital de los Valles, Cumbayá (airport side)
MSP vaccine is normally free (unconfirmed for foreigners). Open question: who in the group has pre-exposure vaccination? Recommended for everyone; it changes the treatment after a bite.

WHAT TO BRING · 1 OF 2
PACKING

Group
packing list

Ecuador uses US plugs (types A/B, 120 V): Bárbara needs an adapter. “Group kit” is one set split between the two cars.
ALTITUDE AND COLD · QUITO, PAPALLACTA PASS, MIRADORES
EACH PERSON
Warm fleece or down layer, waterproof shell, beanie and light gloves (the pass is ~0–9 °C / 32–48 °F), long trousers, closed shoes, SPF 50+ sunscreen and SPF lip balm, sunglasses, hat, refillable bottle.
GROUP KIT
Ibuprofen or paracetamol. Anyone with altitude history: ask a doctor about acetazolamide.
AMAZON HEAT AND RAIN · TENA, MISAHUALLÍ, PUYO
EACH PERSON
Repellent with 20–30% DEET or 20% picaridin; light long sleeves and trousers for dusk; quick-dry clothes (~28 °C / 82 °F and humid); rain jacket or poncho; strapped sandals; zip-bag for the phone; binoculars.
GROUP KIT
2 dry bags (~20 L), one per car; bin bags; anti-itch or antihistamine cream.
HOT SPRINGS AND POOLS · TENA, BAÑOS
EACH PERSON
Swimsuits, flip-flops, quick-dry towel, a warm layer for after (Baños nights ~13 °C / 55 °F), swim cap if you own one (sold at the Termas, ~$1–2).
GROUP KIT
A mesh or wet bag per car.
THE ONE RULE
Jackets, hats and gloves ride in the cabin, not the boot: Sun 29 Nov swings ~25 °C between the pass and Tena in five hours.
WHAT TO BRING · 2 OF 2
PACKING

Group
packing list

Night walk kit and what lives in each car on the five road days (28, 29 Nov; 1, 3, 5 Dec).
NIGHT WALK · MINDO, THU 3 DEC
EACH PERSON
Headlamp (red-light mode) if you have it, long sleeves and trousers, closed shoes, rain jacket, repellent (night ~16–18 °C / 61–64 °F, damp). Headlamps and boots are included by the guide.
GROUP KIT
Spare AAA batteries, a small torch per car.
CAR DAYS · 28, 29 NOV · 1, 3, 5 DEC
PER CAR
12 V USB charger and cables, phone mount, offline maps, ~5 L water, snacks, motion-sickness tablets, wet wipes, trash bag, $1 and $5 notes for tolls and parking, jackets in the cabin.
GROUP KIT
First-aid kit (plasters, blister pads, antiseptic, rehydration salts, loperamide, antihistamine), hand sanitiser, FFP2/N95 masks, a power bank per car.
SHOES
Grip for Pailón and the Mindo trails, not sandals. Strapped sandals for the canoe.
CASH
Small entries, canoes and stalls are cash. $1 coins for tolls; $1, $5, $10 bills for taxis.
MEDICINES
See the Recommended medicines card; prescriptions in original packaging, in carry-on.
TO ASK THE HOSTS
Tena and Mindo: are there boots to lend? (Louisa asks.)
HOW TO BEHAVE · WHAT TO SAY
ETIQUETTE

Manners,
words, tips

“Buenos días / buenas tardes” walking into any shop, taxi or community. In a community, greet the host or elders first and follow their lead.
SPANISH
Con permiso excuse me
¿Me regala…? could I have…?
¿Puedo tomarle una foto? may I take your photo?
¿Cuánto cuesta? how much?
¿Me hace una rebajita? a small discount?
Muy amable very kind
¡Qué rico! delicious!
Gracias, ya no thanks, no more (chicha)
KICHWA
Alli puncha good morning
Alli chishi good afternoon
Yupaychani thank you (highlands, Saquisilí)
Pagarachu thank you (Napo)
SLANG YOU’LL HEAR
¡Achachay! it’s cold
¡Arrarray! it’s hot
guagua baby
ñaño / ñaña brother / sister
¿Mande? pardon?
De ley for sure
PHOTOS
Ask first and accept a no. A purchase or $1 if someone poses at your request. Never children without a parent’s OK. No drones over communities. No photos inside La Compañía.
BARGAINING
Gently (~10–20% off) at Saquisilí, crafts only, and La Mariscal. Not at Sinchi Warmi, co-ops (Kallari, Tianguez), fixed-price shops or food stalls.
TIPPING · CASH
Restaurants add 10% servicio on top of 15% IVA: round up for great service, ~10% if there’s no servicio. Guides ~$5–10 pp per day · boat drivers ~$2–5 pp · taxis round up · porters $1–2 a bag · house cleaners optional $5–10.
Churches: no hats, don’t walk around during Mass. Chicha: a small sip, hand the bowl back. Say no to any limpia or ayahuasca add-on. Cuy and chontacuro: no joke photos in front of the cooks.
WHAT TO PACK · A GENERAL LIST
MEDICINES

Medicines

“Group kit” is one set split between the two cars; “own” means each person brings it. Rx = prescription.
MEDICINE

Paracetamol or ibuprofen
Headache, fever, aches; the usual altitude headache. Ibuprofen with food; not with ulcers or kidney problems.

Helps prevent altitude sickness. Not with a sulfa allergy; tingling fingers and peeing more are normal.

PHARMACIES

HEALTH BY DAY · FROM THE SHARED DOC
FRI 27 – SAT 28 · QUITO
Quito is at 2,850 m / 9,350 ft: water, little alcohol, early night.
SUN 29 · PAPALLACTA → TENA
At ~4,060 m / 13,320 ft, no exertion; anyone with a headache rests in the car. Dengue in Napo: repellent by day.
MON 30 · TENA
Bite or scratch (any mammal): wash 15 minutes, then the same day to Hospital General José María Velasco Ibarra, Tena (MSP, 24 h).
TUE 1 – WED 2 · BAÑOS
No alcohol with the hot pools. Tungurahua: check igepn.edu.ec the week before. Hospital Básico Baños (24 h); Ambato (~40 km / 25 mi) for anything serious.
THU 3 – FRI 4 · MINDO
Nearest care: Centro de Salud Mindo (basic); Hospital Metropolitano, Quito, ~80 km / 50 mi (~2 h).
SAT 5 · AIRPORT
Nearest hospital on the airport side: Hospital de los Valles, Cumbayá (~20 km / 12 mi).
WHO LIVES HERE · 1 OF 2
CULTURE

The culture
you’ll meet

The 2008 Constitution makes Ecuador “plurinational”: 14 Indigenous nationalities and 18 peoples alongside the mestizo majority and Afro-Ecuadorians. Kichwa is an official language of intercultural relations.
ECUADOR IN ONE MINUTE
·
The Indigenous movement (CONAIE) is a real political force: its road blockades shut the country in 2019 and 2022.
·
The Constitution includes sumak kawsay (“good living”) and the Rights of Nature, a world first. In 2023 voters stopped oil drilling in part of Yasuní; you’ll drive through oil country to Tena.
QUITO · 27–28 NOV · COLONIAL GOLD AND A CITY FIESTA
·
Refounded by the Spanish on 6 Dec 1534. In 1978 its Historic Centre was among the first two places on the UNESCO list.
·
La Compañía: gold leaf over almost everything, Moorish ceilings, local fruit and faces among the saints. This is the Escuela Quiteña, mostly Indigenous and mestizo artists (Caspicara, Legarda). At San Francisco, Andean sun symbols mix with Christian ones.
·
Fiestas de Quito (since 1959): chivas, canelazo, wooden-cart races, games of cuarenta and “El Chulla Quiteño”. A chulla is the proud, broke, well-dressed Quito bohemian.
·
Pululahua is one of the few inhabited volcanic craters in the world.
NAPO KICHWA · 29–30 NOV · THE AMAZON, RUN BY WOMEN
·
The chakra is a forest garden of cacao, yuca, guayusa and medicinal plants. FAO heritage system since 2023; ~80% are run by women (chakramamas).
·
Guayusa is drunk at 03:00–04:00 to share dreams and plan the day. Maito means “wrapped”; chicha de yuca is a gesture of welcome.
·
The black face paint, wituk, lasts up to two weeks: only say yes if you mean it.
·
Chocolate starts here: 5,300-year-old cacao residue from Ecuador’s southern Amazon is the oldest evidence of cacao use found so far.
NEXT → Baños, Saquisilí, Mindo and Tulipe, plus souvenirs and a playlist, on card 2.
WHO LIVES HERE · 2 OF 2
CULTURE

The culture
you’ll meet

Pilgrims and a volcano, a working highland market, and the lost Yumbo people of the cloud forest.
BAÑOS · 1–2 DEC · PILGRIMS, A VOLCANO, SUGAR CANE
·
In the Basílica, look for the ex-voto paintings: buses going off cliffs and eruptions, each with the Virgin of Agua Santa saving the people involved.
·
“Mama Tungurahua” erupted on and off from 1999 to 2016; the evacuation signs are still up. Melcocha and guarapo come from the valley’s sugar cane.
SAQUISILÍ · 3 DEC · A WORKING HIGHLAND MARKET
·
Kichwa families from Cotopaxi restock for the week: men’s ponchos and felt hats, women’s shawls and gold-coloured bead necklaces.
·
Buy a Tigua painting: bright village scenes on sheepskin, a style started in the 1970s by Julio Toaquiza. La Mamá Negra is named after Latacunga’s parade; chugchucaras is the town dish.
MINDO AND TULIPE · 3–5 DEC · THE LOST YUMBO PEOPLE
·
The Yumbos traded between highlands and coast from ~500–800 AD along sunken paths called culuncos. Pichincha’s eruptions, the last major one in 1660, are thought to have ended their way of life.
·
At Tulipe, look at the pool shapes (circles, half-moons, a polygon some link to the jaguar): hypotheses, and ceremonies are still held at the solstices.
SOUVENIRS · YES
Tigua paintings, Kichwa seed jewellery and chocolate (Sinchi Warmi, Kallari), a toquilla straw “Panama” hat (Ecuadorian; UNESCO 2012), tagua nut carvings.
SOUVENIRS · NO
Anything with feathers, teeth, claws, skins or butterflies, and “pre-Columbian” pieces: illegal to export, or fakes.
LISTEN FOR · BEFORE YOU GO
Pasillo (slow, melancholy; Julio Jaramillo) and sanjuanito (the bouncy Andean beat). Optional: Savages by Joe Kane (oil in the Amazon), Crude (2009 documentary), a Julio Jaramillo playlist.
